title: The nuclear atom and isotopes
summary: Every atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus made of [[proton|protons]] and [[neutron|neutrons]], with [[electron|electrons]] in the space around it. All atoms of one [[element|element]] have the same number of protons, but [[isotope|isotopes]] of it have different numbers of neutrons. That is why most [[relative-atomic-mass|relative atomic masses]] are not whole numbers.

goals.text: Describe the nuclear atom, and state the relative mass and charge of the proton, neutron and electron.
Read a nuclear symbol $\ce{^{A}_{Z}X}$ to count the protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or an [[ion|ion]].
Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.
Calculate a relative atomic mass from isotope masses and abundances, and work backwards to an abundance or an isotope mass.
Interpret a [[mass-spectrum|mass spectrum]] to identify the isotopes of an element, their relative abundances and its relative atomic mass.

before.prompt: Which of these substances is an element?
before.hint: An element cannot be broken down chemically into anything simpler.
before.explain: Copper cannot be broken down chemically. Water and carbon dioxide are [[compound|compounds]], and brass is a [[mixture|mixture]] of copper and zinc. Revise it in {{lesson:1.1}}.

before.prompt: Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, but no chemical reaction splits hydrogen into anything simpler. What does this show?
before.hint: Ask which substance can be broken down chemically.

options.text: water is a compound and hydrogen is an element
water is an element and hydrogen is a compound
water and hydrogen are both mixtures

before.explain: Water breaks down chemically into two elements, so it is a compound. Hydrogen cannot be broken down, so it is an element. Revise it in {{lesson:1.1}}.

verify.truth: water is a compound and hydrogen is an element

blocks.text: Almost all of an atom's mass sits in a tiny centre called the nucleus. The rest of the atom is mostly empty space.

The nucleus holds two kinds of particle: [[proton|protons]], which are positive, and [[neutron|neutrons]], which have no charge. [[electron|Electrons]] are negative, and they occupy the space outside the nucleus.

blocks.statement: A proton or a neutron: either of the two particles found in the nucleus.
blocks.plain: The particles the nucleus is built from.

blocks.alt: Model of a lithium-7 atom, not to scale. A tiny nucleus in the centre holds 3 protons, each marked plus, and 4 neutrons with no charge. Around it, a large shaded region of mostly empty space holds 3 electrons, each marked minus.
blocks.caption: A lithium-7 atom. Real nuclei are far smaller than this.

blocks.text: Learn the relative masses and charges. Proton: mass 1, charge $+1$. Neutron: mass 1, charge 0. Electron: mass about $\tfrac{1}{1836}$, charge $-1$.

The actual values are in section 2 of the data booklet. The electron's mass is negligible, so an atom's mass is in effect the mass of its nucleus. With that mass packed into a tiny volume, the nucleus is extremely dense.
An atom has as many electrons as protons, so the charges cancel and the atom is neutral.

blocks.statement: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, symbol $Z$.
blocks.plain: Every atom with 6 protons is carbon.

blocks.text: The [[atomic-number|atomic number]] fixes the element. Each element's $Z$ is printed in the periodic table (data booklet, section 7).

blocks.statement: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom, symbol $A$.
blocks.plain: Count the heavy particles in the nucleus.

blocks.text: A nuclear symbol puts both numbers on the element's symbol: $\ce{^{A}_{Z}X}$. The mass number goes top left, the atomic number bottom left, and any charge top right.

blocks.statement: An atom or group of atoms with an overall charge, because its number of electrons differs from its number of protons.
blocks.plain: A positive ion has lost electrons; a negative ion has gained them.

blocks.text: Forming an [[ion|ion]] changes only the electrons. A $2+$ ion has 2 fewer electrons than protons, and a $3-$ ion has 3 more.

blocks.alt: The nuclear symbol of a sodium ion: Na with 23 at the top left, labelled mass number A equals protons plus neutrons, 11 at the bottom left, labelled atomic number Z equals protons, and a plus sign at the top right, labelled charge, one electron lost. Beside it: protons 11, neutrons 23 minus 11 equals 12, electrons 11 minus 1 equals 10.

blocks.question: An atom of fluorine has the nuclear symbol $\ce{^{19}_{9}F}$. Describe its structure, including the number, position and charge of each type of particle.
steps: Protons: $Z = 9$.
Neutrons: $A - Z = 19 - 9 = 10$.
Electrons: the atom is neutral, so 9.
Then say where each particle is and its charge.
blocks.answer: The atom has a small, dense nucleus that contains 9 protons and 10 neutrons. Each proton has a charge of +1 and each neutron has no charge, so the nucleus is positive. 9 electrons, each with a charge of -1, occupy the space outside the nucleus. The 9 positive and 9 negative charges cancel, so the atom is neutral.

verify.truth: nucleus of 9 protons and 10 neutrons; 9 electrons outside the nucleus; neutral

blocks.question: State the numbers of protons ($p$), neutrons ($n$) and electrons ($e$) in the ion $\ce{^{52}_{24}Cr^3+}$.
steps: Protons: $p = Z = 24$.
Neutrons: $n = A - Z = 52 - 24 = 28$.
The charge is $3+$, so the atom has lost 3 electrons: $e = 24 - 3 = 21$.
Check: $p - e = 24 - 21 = 3$, which matches the charge.

blocks.prompt: How many electrons are in the ion $\ce{^{31}_{15}P^3-}$?
blocks.hint: A negative charge means electrons were gained.
blocks.explain: Phosphorus has $Z = 15$, so the atom has 15 electrons. A $3-$ ion has gained 3 more: $15 + 3 = 18$.

blocks.prompt: A species has 20 protons, 22 neutrons and 18 electrons. Its nuclear symbol is $\ce{^{A}_{Z}X}$ with charge $q$. Which values are correct?
blocks.hint: Protons give $Z$. Protons plus neutrons give $A$. Compare protons with electrons for the charge.
blocks.explain: $Z = 20$, so it is calcium. $A = 20 + 22 = 42$. It has 2 fewer electrons than protons, so $q = +2$: $\ce{^{42}_{20}Ca^2+}$.

blocks.text: Most carbon atoms have 6 neutrons, but about 1 in 100 has 7. Both are carbon, because both have 6 protons.

blocks.statement: Atoms of the same element, so with the same number of protons, that have different numbers of neutrons.

blocks.text: So [[isotope|isotopes]] share an [[atomic-number|atomic number]] but not a mass number. Carbon-12 is $\ce{^{12}_{6}C}$ and carbon-13 is $\ce{^{13}_{6}C}$.
Reactions involve electrons. Isotopes have the same number of electrons in the same arrangement, so they react in the same way.

Properties that depend on mass differ. A substance made with a heavier isotope is denser, and at the same temperature its particles move and diffuse more slowly. Melting and boiling points can differ slightly, and some isotopes are radioactive.
You don't need to learn particular isotopes: questions give you the data.

blocks.statement: Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.
blocks.why: Chemistry depends on the electrons, which isotopes share. Mass depends on the neutrons, which they don't.

blocks.question: Oxygen has three stable isotopes: $\ce{^{16}_{8}O}$, $\ce{^{17}_{8}O}$ and $\ce{^{18}_{8}O}$. State the number of neutrons in each, in that order.
steps: All three have $Z = 8$: 8 protons, and 8 electrons in the atom.
Only the neutron count changes. That is exactly what makes them isotopes.

blocks.question: Methane can be made with carbon-12 or with carbon-13. Explain why both kinds of methane burn in oxygen to give the same products, but have different densities.
steps: Chemistry: same electrons, so the same reactions.
Density: one more neutron, so a greater mass.
blocks.answer: Carbon-12 and carbon-13 both have 6 protons and 6 electrons, so they have the same electron configuration. Chemical reactions depend on the electrons, so both kinds of methane react with oxygen in the same way and give the same products. A carbon-13 atom has one more neutron than a carbon-12 atom, so methane made from carbon-13 has a greater molecular mass. Density depends on mass, so the carbon-13 methane is denser.

verify.truth: same electrons so same chemistry; extra neutron so greater mass and density

blocks.prompt: Which pair are isotopes of each other?
blocks.hint: Isotopes are the same element with different mass numbers.

options.text: a sodium-23 atom and a sodium-23 ion

blocks.explain: Both are neon, with 10 protons, but they have 10 and 12 neutrons. Argon-40 and calcium-40 are different elements. A sodium atom and its ion differ only in electrons.

blocks.prompt: Nitrogen gas can be made from nitrogen-14 or from nitrogen-15. Which property is different for the two gases?
blocks.hint: Which properties depend on electrons, and which on mass?

options.text: the number of electrons in each molecule
the number of bonds between the two atoms
the product formed when it reacts with hydrogen

blocks.explain: Same electrons means the same bonding and reactions. Nitrogen-15 molecules are heavier, so that gas is denser.

blocks.text: Most elements are a mixture of isotopes, so their average atomic mass lies between the isotope masses, closest to the commonest one.
Masses are measured against carbon-12, set at exactly 12. On this scale an isotope's mass is its relative isotopic mass, very close to its mass number.

blocks.statement: The weighted mean mass of the atoms of an element, relative to one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Symbol $A_\text{r}$.
blocks.plain: The average mass of the element's atoms, counting each isotope by how common it is.

blocks.text: [[relative-atomic-mass|Relative atomic mass]] has no units, because it compares two masses. Because it averages the isotopes, it is rarely a whole number. The data booklet lists it in section 7.
Multiply each mass by its abundance, add, then divide by 100. The answer must lie between the lightest and heaviest isotope masses.

blocks.question: A sample of gallium is 60.11% gallium-69 (relative isotopic mass 68.93) and 39.89% gallium-71 (relative isotopic mass 70.92). Calculate the relative atomic mass of gallium, to two decimal places.
steps: Multiply each mass by its abundance: $68.93 \times 60.11 = 4143.3823$ and $70.92 \times 39.89 = 2829.0988$.
Round only at the end. It is nearer 69 than 71, as gallium-69 is commoner.

blocks.text: To work backwards from $A_\text{r}$, call one abundance $x\%$. The other is then $(100 - x)\%$.

blocks.question: Rubidium has two isotopes: rubidium-85 (relative isotopic mass 84.912) and rubidium-87 (relative isotopic mass 86.909). Use the $A_\text{r}$ of rubidium in section 7 of the data booklet to calculate the percentage abundance of rubidium-87, to 3 significant figures.
steps: From the data booklet (section 7), $A_\text{r}(\ce{Rb}) = 85.47$.
Let rubidium-87 be $x\%$, so rubidium-85 is $(100 - x)\%$.
Set up the weighted mean: $\frac{84.912(100 - x) + 86.909x}{100} = 85.47$.
Check: rubidium-85 is then $72.1\%$, which fits $A_\text{r}$ being nearer 85.

blocks.prompt: Antimony has $A_\text{r} = 121.76$ and two isotopes. Antimony-121 has relative isotopic mass 120.90 and abundance 57.21%. Calculate the relative isotopic mass of the other isotope, to two decimal places.
blocks.hint: The other isotope makes up $100 - 57.21 = 42.79\%$. Call its mass $m$ and set up the weighted mean.

blocks.prompt: Silicon is 92.23% silicon-28 (relative isotopic mass 27.98), 4.68% silicon-29 (28.98) and 3.09% silicon-30 (29.97). What is its relative atomic mass?
blocks.hint: Weight each mass by its abundance. Don't just average the three masses.

blocks.text: A mass spectrometer turns atoms into positive ions and sorts them by mass-to-charge ratio, $m/z$. How it works is not assessed.
The output is a [[mass-spectrum|mass spectrum]]: relative abundance against $m/z$. Most ions carry a $1+$ charge, so $m/z$ is the ion's relative mass.

blocks.statement: In the mass spectrum of an element, each peak from a single-atom ion is one isotope. Its $m/z$ gives the isotope's relative mass, and its height gives the isotope's relative abundance.
blocks.why: Ions of equal charge are sorted by mass alone, and a commoner isotope makes more ions.

blocks.alt: Mass spectrum of magnesium. The horizontal axis is m over z, from 23 to 27; the vertical axis is relative abundance, from 0 to 100. Three vertical lines: at 24 with height 100, at 25 with height 12.66, and at 26 with height 13.94.
blocks.caption: Magnesium: three isotopes, scaled so the tallest peak is 100.

blocks.text: Percentage abundances add up to 100. Heights scaled to a tallest peak of 100 add up to more, so divide by their total.

blocks.question: The mass spectrum of an element shows two peaks: $m/z = 63$ with abundance 69.2% and $m/z = 65$ with abundance 30.8%. Calculate its $A_\text{r}$ to two decimal places, and use section 7 of the data booklet to identify the element.
steps: The abundances add up to 100, so divide by 100: $A_\text{r} = \frac{63 \times 69.2 + 65 \times 30.8}{100} = \frac{4359.6 + 2002}{100} = 63.616$.
Section 7: copper is 63.55 and zinc 65.38, so the element is copper. Using mass numbers explains the small difference.

blocks.question: The figure shows the mass spectrum of magnesium, scaled so the tallest peak is 100. Determine the relative atomic mass of magnesium, to two decimal places.
steps: Read the peaks: $m/z$ 24 (height 100), 25 (12.66) and 26 (13.94).
The heights do not add up to 100. Their total is $100 + 12.66 + 13.94 = 126.60$.
Check: about 79% of the atoms are magnesium-24, so just above 24 makes sense.

blocks.text: In a Paper 1A spectrum question, add up the peak heights before you divide. Divide by 100 only if they total 100.

Diatomic elements, such as the halogens, also show molecule peaks at higher $m/z$, one for each pair of isotopes. With two equally common isotopes, a mixed molecule forms two ways (light–heavy or heavy–light), so the three peaks are $1:2:1$.

blocks.prompt: The mass spectrum of lithium has a peak at $m/z = 6$ of height 8.1 and a peak at $m/z = 7$ of height 100. Calculate the relative atomic mass of lithium, to two decimal places.
blocks.hint: The heights add up to $108.1$, not 100.

blocks.prompt: Element Q has two isotopes, of mass numbers $a$ and $a + 2$, in equal amounts. It forms $\ce{Q2}$ molecules. What do the molecular peaks in its mass spectrum look like?
blocks.hint: List every way to pick two atoms, one after the other. How many ways give the mixed molecule?

options.text: three peaks, with the middle one twice as tall as the others

blocks.explain: The molecules are light–light ($2a$), light–heavy or heavy–light ($2a + 2$), and heavy–heavy ($2a + 4$). The middle mass forms in two ways, so its peak is twice as tall.

verify.truth: three peaks, with the middle one twice as tall as the others

blocks.text: Proton: relative mass 1, charge $+1$. Neutron: relative mass 1, charge 0. Electron: negligible mass, charge $-1$. Protons and neutrons are in the tiny, dense nucleus; electrons are outside it.
In $\ce{^{A}_{Z}X}$, protons $= Z$. In an ion, electrons $= Z -$ charge: subtract for a positive ion, add for a negative one.
Isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons but different numbers of neutrons. They have the same chemical properties but different physical properties.
In a mass spectrum, each peak is an isotope: $m/z$ gives its mass and the height its abundance. If the heights don't total 100, divide by their sum.

mistakes: Putting the wrong atomic number in a nuclear symbol. Take $Z$ from the periodic table (data booklet, section 7) and write it bottom left.
Adding electrons for a positive ion. A $2+$ ion has lost two electrons: subtract the charge from $Z$.
Writing the data-booklet $A_\text{r}$ when asked to calculate it from given data. Show the weighted mean; the booklet value alone earns nothing.
Averaging isotope masses without weighting. Multiply each mass by its abundance first.
Saying isotopes have different chemical properties. Same electrons means the same reactions.
In mass spectra (HL), dividing by 100 when the peak heights don't total 100. Divide by their sum.
examTips: "State" the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons: no working needed, but check that protons minus electrons equals the charge.
"Calculate" $A_\text{r}$: write the weighted mean with the numbers substituted, then the answer to the precision asked.
"Distinguish" between two isotopes in one sentence: the same number of protons, but a different number of neutrons.
